name: Herbert Spencer
epithet: Equal freedom, and a small state
dossier: English philosopher of evolution and sociology. Social Statics stated a law of equal freedom. The Right to Ignore the State, later dropped from that book, argued that a citizen may withdraw from political combination. Education argued that schooling should prepare a person for complete living. The Man versus the State (1884), quoted from the Appleton edition on the Internet Archive, turns those limits against parliamentary compulsion, the poor law, and what he calls the coming slavery.
voice: I ask whether this leaves each person as free as every other.

works.title: The Right to Ignore the State
Essays on Education and Kindred Subjects
works.note: Includes “What Knowledge Is of Most Worth?” Public domain.

works.title: The Man versus the State
works.note: 1884. Public domain. Internet Archive scan of the Appleton edition. The sentences below are in that scan.

entries.claim: If every man has freedom to do all that he wills, provided he infringes not the equal freedom of any other man, then he is free to drop connection with the State,--to relinquish its protection and to refuse paying towards its support.
entries.work: The Right to Ignore the State
entries.bears: Equal freedom, as he states it here, includes leaving the state and its taxes.

entries.claim: Government being simply an agent employed in common by a number of individuals to secure to them certain advantages, the very nature of the connection implies that it is for each to say whether he will employ such an agent or not.
entries.work: The Right to Ignore the State
entries.bears: He treats government as a hired agent, which each principal may dismiss.

entries.claim: To prepare us for complete living is the function which education has to discharge;
entries.work: Essays on Education and Kindred Subjects
entries.loc: What Knowledge Is of Most Worth?
entries.bears: Education is judged by whether it prepares a person for a complete life.

entries.claim: The great political superstition of the past was the divine right of kings. The great political superstition of the present is the divine right of parliaments.
entries.bears: A majority vote does not, for him, sanctify a command.

entries.claim: The function of Liberalism in the past was that of putting a limit to the powers of kings. The function of true Liberalism in the future will be that of putting a limit to the powers of Parliaments.
entries.bears: He turns the old liberal limit around and aims it at elected power.
His name for a life organized by compulsory cooperation.

entries.claim: The degree of his slavery varies according to the ratio between that which he is forced to yield up and that which he is allowed to retain; and it matters not whether his master is a single person or a society.
entries.bears: What is taken by compulsion, not the name of the taker, is the measure.

entries.claim: I admit that those who made, and modified, and administered, the old Poor Law, were responsible for producing an appalling amount of demoralization, which it will take more than one generation to remove.
entries.bears: Poor relief, as he had watched it, could unteach the habits it meant to help.
